PASSO 1: ouça «Ich heiße Lea.» e depois: STEP 1: listen to «Ich heiße Lea.» and then «Wie heißt du?». To say your name, the verb is «heißen», "to be called" — German says "I am called Lea", not "my name is". STEP 2: in German, the conjugated verb is always in SECOND position in the sentence. In «Ich heiße Lea», «ich» takes first position and «heiße» second. STEP 3: in questions with a question word, that word comes first. Examples: «wie», which means "how" and sounds like «vee», and «woher», which means "where from" and sounds like «voh-HEHR». The verb stays second: «Wie heißt du?» and «Woher kommst du?». STEP 4: in a yes/no question, the verb moves to the front: «Heißt du Lea?» — no "do" needed, unlike English. Answer «Ja» or «Nein». STEP 5: the verb ending changes with the person. With «ich», it ends in «e»: «ich heiße», «ich komme». With «du», it ends in «st»: «du kommst». In «heißen», the «ß» already makes the «s» sound, so you only add «t»: «du heißt». STEP 6: as in English, the pronoun is required: «Ich komme aus den USA», never just «Komme aus den USA». STEP 7: a heads-up. In «der Name» and «der Vorname», «der» is an article (a German "the"). You'll learn the articles in lesson 3. For now, repeat «der» together with the word.
em português o verbo também vem logo dep: English and German start out alike: «Ich heiße Lea», "I am called Lea". The difference shows up as soon as something else opens the sentence. English keeps subject-then-verb ("Today I come"), but German keeps the verb in second place no matter what comes first: «Heute komme ich», literally "Today come I". English has a trace of this in questions ("Where are you from?"), and German questions work the same way: «Woher kommst du?». One more trap: «Wer» means "who", not "where" — "where" is «wo».

PASSO 1: em português temos dois verbos,: STEP 1: German "to be" is «sein», pronounced «zine». STEP 2: «sein» is irregular and changes a lot, just like "am, are, is". Listen to the forms: «ich bin», «du bist», «er, sie, es ist», «wir sind», «ihr seid», «sie sind». Careful: «sind» sounds like «zint» and «seid» like «zite». STEP 3: use «sein» to say who you are: «Ich bin Amerikaner» or «Das ist Lea». STEP 4: use it also to say how or where you are: «Ich bin müde» and «Wir sind hier». STEP 5: to make it negative, put «nicht» after the verb: «Ich bin nicht müde» — like "I am not tired". STEP 6: in a yes/no question, the verb moves to the front: «Bist du müde?», "Are you tired?". Answer: «Ja, ich bin müde.» or «Nein, ich bin nicht müde.»
o português tem dois verbos, «ser» e «es: «sein» is the German "to be", and it behaves almost exactly like it: one verb for who you are and how or where you are, irregular in every person, just as "am, are, is" are. Match them up and they stick: «ich bin» (I am), «du bist» (you are), «er ist» (he is). One trap: German says «Ich bin müde» (I'm tired), but for cold, hunger and age it often switches verbs — «Mir ist kalt», not «Ich bin kalt», which would mean you're a cold person. You'll meet those later.

O verbo fica na segunda posição, e o «ni: The verb stays in second position, and «nicht» comes after it.
Você, vocês, o senhor: du, ihr e Sie: Three ways to say "you": du, ihr and Sie
PASSO 1: para falar com UMA pessoa próxi: STEP 1: to talk to ONE person you're close to — a friend, family member, child or young classmate — use «du». STEP 2: to talk to SEVERAL people you're close to, use «ihr», like "you guys" or "y'all". STEP 3: to talk to someone you don't know well, or to show respect, use «Sie», pronounced «zee». It covers sir, ma'am, and any group addressed formally. In writing, formal «Sie» always starts with a capital S. STEP 4: with «Sie» the verb takes the same form as «sie» (they): «Sie sind» and «Wie heißen Sie?». STEP 5: when in doubt, use «Sie». The other person will offer you «du» when they want to — and in German that's a real moment, not a formality.
em português, «você» serve para quase to: English has one "you" for everyone. German has three, and the choice is not optional: «du» for one friend, «ihr» for several (like "you guys" or "y'all"), and «Sie» for anyone you'd call Mr. or Ms. Using «du» with a stranger, a shop clerk or your boss sounds rude in Germany. And the choice changes the verb: «Wie heißt du?» but «Wie heißen Sie?».

PASSO 1: para dizer de onde você vem, us: STEP 1: to say where you're from, use «Ich komme aus» and the country: «Ich komme aus Kanada». STEP 2: most countries take no article: «Kanada», «England», «Deutschland». A few do, and you learn them as fixed phrases: «Ich komme aus den USA», «Ich komme aus der Schweiz». You'll understand why later. STEP 3: for a man's nationality, use «Amerikaner». For a woman, add «in»: «Amerikanerin». STEP 4: after «sein», the nationality takes no article — unlike English "I'm an American": «Ich bin Amerikaner». STEP 5: languages take no article either, and they're capitalized, as in English: «Ich spreche Deutsch». STEP 6: the verb «sprechen» (to speak) is irregular with «du» and «er»: «ich spreche», «du sprichst», «er spricht». The «sp» at the start sounds like «shp», as you saw in lesson 1.
em português usamos uma palavra para a p: English often uses one word for the person and the language ("German", "Spanish"). German keeps three apart: the country «Deutschland», the person «Deutscher / Deutsche», and the language «Deutsch». Two English habits to drop: no article before a nationality — "I'm an American" is «Ich bin Amerikaner», never «ein Amerikaner» — and a woman adds «-in»: «Amerikanerin», «Engländerin», «Kanadierin».
Para nacionalidade, o natural é dizer se: For nationality, German uses no article — unlike English "I'm an American".
